extracted.intended_audience: applicants to and evaluators of European Research Council (ERC) research grant calls; ERC Scientific Council and panel members
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluation standards for assessing ERC research proposals and applicants, including new 2024 changes to application templates, evaluation order, weighting, and permitted evidence in narrative CVs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sole criterion: scientific excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals will continue to be evaluated on the sole criterion of scientific excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels primarily evaluate the ground-breaking nature, ambition, and feasibility of the research project. Economic or societal impact should not be used as an explicit evaluation criterion for ERC grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project: ground-breaking nature, ambition, feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The project evaluation focuses on its ground-breaking nature, the ambition of the objectives, and the feasibility of the proposed approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'ambitious', 'creative and original' rather than 'high-risk, high-gain'. Evaluate core questions and approaches rather than specific elements like methodology-development unless central to the proposal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant: intellectual capacity and creativity
rubrics_metrics.description: Panels evaluate the intellectual capacity and creativity of the applicant, focusing on whether the applicant has the scientific expertise and capacity to successfully execute the project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment is based primarily on the track record (research outputs) and peer recognition, with additional information used for context. Applicant evaluation is qualitative (outstanding / excellent / very good / good / non-competitive) and not numerically combined with the project score.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation order: project-first remote evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: During individual remote evaluation, panel members first evaluate the research project without considering applicant information and decide a project score, then evaluate the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is to avoid the applicant's identity/reputation influencing the project score and to reduce unconscious bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring and weighting: numeric project score; qualitative applicant assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Only the project is scored on a numerical scale (1–5) and used to rank proposals prior to panel discussion; the applicant receives an overall qualitative assessment (five options) that is not converted to a number or combined with the project score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This change gives stronger emphasis to project quality in initial rankings and reduces risk of Matthew effects from institutional reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combined CV and track record template (4 pages)
rubrics_metrics.description: The CV and track record are combined into a single template limited to four pages (fixed font/spacing). Applicants decide allocation of space among the three sections: personal details; research achievements and peer recognition; additional information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limitations and fixed length constrain narrative excess and force prioritisation; applicants should explain significance of selected outputs in neutral factual terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit research outputs to up to ten with narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: For research achievements, applicants may list up to ten examples of research outputs, with an emphasis on more recent ones, and are encouraged to provide brief narratives explaining how each advanced the field and demonstrates capacity to carry out the proposed project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Type of output is deliberately left open (publications, preprints, books, datasets, code, expeditions, artefacts, etc.). Focus on quality and significance rather than quantity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow diverse types of research outputs
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise a wide range of research outputs beyond traditional publications: datasets, open-source code/software, expeditions, patents, prototypes, exhibitions, policy contributions, open peer reviews, educational products, clinical guidelines, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants may list outputs in any format relevant to their field; panels are instructed to focus on scientific content rather than format or venue prestige.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative CV elements: neutral factual explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative elements should be brief, factual explanations of the significance of selected outputs, the applicant's role in producing them, and how they demonstrate capacity to carry out the proposed project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructions emphasise neutral wording to reduce boastful self-presentation; narratives are voluntary and intended to complement objective evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use inappropriate quantitative proxies (e.g., Journal Impact Factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluators must refrain from using surrogate quantitative metrics such as Journal Impact Factors as proxies for quality of research outputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantitative metrics must be used responsibly; panels should focus on scientific content and quality of outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer recognition evidence (open-ended)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may list evidence of peer recognition (prizes, awards, academy memberships, leadership positions), without prescriptive required elements, and use narratives to explain context and significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because such items vary greatly by field and career stage, the template leaves choices open and asks for contextual explanations where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional information section for context
rubrics_metrics.description: A section where applicants can provide information on career breaks, diverse career paths, major life events, and particularly noteworthy contributions to the research community not reflected elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This information provides context to panels but does not directly enter as scored elements of the track record; panels consider it when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not ask for supervision counts as mentorship metric
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of PhD students or postdocs supervised is no longer requested as it is an unreliable proxy for mentorship quality and is confounded by field and institutional differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numbers alone are insufficient; no practical, fair measure of mentorship was identified for large-scale assessment, so the element was removed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extramural funding treated cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: Information on extramural funding is not used as a primary measure of researcher quality; it is only considered to ensure the proposed project is not already funded and only at a later stage of evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funding success is affected by national contexts and opportunities; it is a proxy that can be misleading as a measure of research importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not require profiles or strict time windows for outputs
rubrics_metrics.description: The old 'profiles' and rigid time windows (e.g., last 10 years for Advanced Grant) have been removed; applicants provide up to ten outputs with emphasis on recency, and panels judge which recent period is appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This change reduces bias against career breaks and diverse career trajectories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other contributions listed for context but not scored
rubrics_metrics.description: Particularly noteworthy contributions to teaching, peer review, community service, or other activities may be listed to provide context, but they do not directly enter the scored evaluation of research achievements and peer recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognises importance of service to research system while avoiding penalising researchers who spend time on such activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'high-risk, high-gain' phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'high-risk, high-gain' is removed from guidance as confusing; 'ambitious', 'creative and original' are preferred descriptors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frontier research inherently involves unpredictability; evaluators should consider ambition and originality without overemphasising risk labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Development of novel methodologies not a required element
rubrics_metrics.description: Development of novel methodologies is neither necessary nor sufficient for a proposal to be excellent and is therefore not specifically asked about in project evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While new methods can be crucial, projects using existing methodologies in original ways can also be excellent; focus on core questions and approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative CV limitations to reduce subjectivity and gaming
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative CVs can be subjective, culture-dependent, and favour strong writers; to mitigate this, the CV/track record section is limited in length and narratives are requested to be neutral and factual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels are wary of boastful applications; space constraints force prioritisation of the most relevant achievements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel guidance should not be overly prescriptive
rubrics_metrics.description: While panels require guidance to ensure fairness and comparability across panels, instructions should avoid being so prescriptive as to constrain applicants' freedom to present work as they deem appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance is needed between fair comparability and panel autonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness and transparency of evaluation process
rubrics_metrics.description: The evaluation process must be as fair and transparent as possible; applicants and panel members should understand what is expected and how information will be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Written guidance and briefings are provided to panels; explicit instruction on evaluation elements helps level the playing field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel member selection and bias mitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Careful selection of panel members and attention to panel structure are important to reduce biases and 'scientific community games'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consideration was given to whether chairs/co-chairs could be Scientific Officers and to other structural reforms, though views differ on Agency staff participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of alternative mechanisms (partial randomisation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Partial randomisation for proposals in 'grey areas' may be considered as a mechanism to address subjectivity and encourage risk-taking research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some funders have used partial randomisation for borderline proposals; the ERC discussed but did not adopt this broadly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of Open Science, EDI, integrity, collegiality (contextual)
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles like Open Science, Equality, Diversity and Inclusion, integrity, collegiality and transparency are important in research culture and may be recognised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While valuable, such elements are not necessarily essential to carry out the project and should be considered carefully; may be used for context or tiebreaking rather than core scoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using host institution prestige as evaluation element
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant's host institution should not enter the evaluation of the applicant's excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduces Matthew effects favouring researchers at highly visible institutions; panels must judge excellence by outputs and recognition rather than institutional affiliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicants responsible for selecting and explaining outputs
rubrics_metrics.description: Responsibility for selecting which outputs and elements of peer recognition to list, and for explaining them, rests with the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels rely on applicants' neutral factual explanations to understand the importance and relevance of the listed items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit on length and fixed formatting of CV to promote comparability
rubrics_metrics.description: The CV/track record template has fixed font and spacing and a four-page limit to promote comparability and control verbosity across applicants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must prioritise and present concise factual descriptions of selected outputs and recognitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panels to focus on scientific content over heuristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Panels should avoid developing their own heuristics that differ across panels and may be sub-optimal; provided guidance aims to reduce such divergence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Briefings and written guidance address frequently asked topics and issues raised during panel briefings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual reporting of career breaks and non-linear careers
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may report career breaks, unconventional career paths, part-time work, and other personal circumstances in the additional information section for context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels are expected to take such context into account when judging the track record and achievements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not convert applicant qualitative assessment into numeric score
rubrics_metrics.description: The five-category qualitative assessment for applicants is not converted into a numerical score and is not combined with the project's numerical score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prevents applicant reputation from directly boosting initial project rankings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check for double-funding / ensure project not already funded
rubrics_metrics.description: Extramural funding information is used to ensure the proposed project is not already funded from other sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This check is conducted at the second step of evaluation rather than as an indicator of applicant quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage applicants to explain role in collaborative outputs
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants should explain their individual role in listed outputs to help panels judge their contribution and capacity to carry out the proposed project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particularly important for multi-author outputs and collaborative projects to understand the applicant's specific contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reaffirmation that excellence is comparative and field-relative
rubrics_metrics.description: Excellence is assessed by whether a proposal or researcher ranks highly in comparison with others, recognising field differences and career stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels must consider field norms and career stage when judging outputs and recognitions; not expecting applicants to satisfy every element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel autonomy within overall guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: While guidance exists, the 90 peer review panels decide independently on final rankings, and panels retain freedom to act according to their expert insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance seeks to harmonise standards without being overly prescriptive; panels may still request clarification or supplementary guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage responsible use of quantitative indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Where metrics are used, they must be applied responsibly and not as surrogate measures of quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels are instructed to prioritise reading and assessing scientific content over relying on bibliometrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of disciplinary differences in peer recognition practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Panels are instructed to be aware that practices like prizes, keynote invitations, and publication venues vary across disciplines and career stages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit guidance for evaluators helps them take such differences into account; applicants should contextualise items in narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research achievements emphasise recent outputs where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants are asked to emphasise more recent achievements among their up-to-ten selected outputs, leaving panels to judge what 'recent' means per CV.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This avoids strict cutoffs that disadvantage those with career breaks or returns from other sectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow inclusion of preprints as valid research outputs
rubrics_metrics.description: Preprints are explicitly allowed among the types of accepted research outputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognises that ground-breaking discoveries may sometimes appear first as preprints or in non-traditional outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage description of societal engagement and broader impacts for context
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may list societal engagement, citizen science, industry engagement, policy advice, public outreach, and other broader-society activities for contextual information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such items provide context but do not become core scored elements of scientific excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of innovation leadership and patents as part of track record
rubrics_metrics.description: Innovation leadership and patents may be presented as evidence of scientific/technological impact and innovation capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels consider such items in context and alongside other outputs like publications, datasets, software, and prototypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborations and interdisciplinarity considered
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that an applicant develops or leads multi-, inter-, trans- or cross-disciplinary activities, maintains international collaborations, or engages in intersectoral collaborations is relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should highlight leadership in collaborative projects and relevant roles in interdisciplinary research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advancement and enablement of junior researchers (contextual)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributions to enabling junior researchers — e.g., fostering excellence through others, student completion rates — may be listed as contextual information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because measures vary by discipline and career stage, such indicators are contextual rather than core scored metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching and mentoring activities can be listed for context
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching, training, workshops, supervision, mentoring and development of researchers may be listed as noteworthy contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Important for research culture recognition, but not strictly required for demonstrating capacity to carry out the proposed project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributions to research community and integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Activities such as editing, reviewing, committee work, organising events, and contributions to research integrity and culture may be listed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels recognise their importance; such contributions provide context and may be considered in nuanced ways rather than as direct scoring elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Societal or economic impact noted but not core ERC criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Societal or economic impact may be described but is not an explicit evaluation criterion for ERC grants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ERC retains focus on scientific excellence; impact considerations could disadvantage basic curiosity-driven research if used as core criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Developmental perspective: career-stage sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation should consider applicants' career stage, leadership potential, research independence and maturity, and mobility, recognising differences across career paths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels should judge appropriate expectations relative to career stage and context; leadership potential is contextual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal context and diversity considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Unconventional career paths, career breaks, part-time work, personal circumstances, belonging to underrepresented groups, and diversity factors should be reportable and taken into account for context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels are encouraged to consider these factors to avoid disadvantaging some applicants; equal opportunities and inclusiveness are intended values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics, integrity and security compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: General and research-specific ethics and integrity standards must be met; security issues and freedom of scientific research are relevant contextual considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must comply with applicable ethical and integrity requirements; panels note such compliance when assessing feasibility and appropriateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reputation and recognition by peers
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of reputation and peer recognition (including academy memberships) may be used as context for assessing applicant excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because such recognitions are field-dependent and vary by career stage, applicants should contextualise their significance in narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leadership roles and appointments
rubrics_metrics.description: Elected or appointed leadership positions in the research community (committee membership, steering roles, corporate roles) may be listed as evidence of service and standing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are contextual indicators and not necessarily direct measures of ability to execute the proposed project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excellence through performance of others
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that an applicant fosters others' performance (nurtures talent, supports colleagues) can be listed as contextual info.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels should be cautious interpreting such measures due to institutional and field disparities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain international research collaborations
rubrics_metrics.description: Sustained international collaborations are considered positive evidence of the applicant's research networks and ability to lead collaborative work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should describe roles and outcomes from such collaborations where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to acquire third-party funds
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to win competitive funding and lead funded research projects can be presented, but winning funds is not treated as a primary proxy for excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels consider funding history in context and primarily to check for double-funding of the proposed project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness to innovative evaluation systems (discussion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ERC considered novel evaluation approaches (narrative CVs, partial randomisation, panel structural changes) to improve fairness and reduce bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some mechanisms (narrative CVs, remote project-first scoring) have been adopted or trialled; others remain under discussion.
